page.title: Settings
page.caution: Follow these steps only if you know what you are doing. They are a suggested setup, not a guarantee. At each step, check that it fits your computer, your network and your needs before you continue.
page.secrets.windows: Passwords and keys are kept in Windows Credential Manager.
page.secrets.darwin: Passwords and keys are kept in your Mac's Keychain.
page.secrets.linux: Passwords and keys are kept in your desktop's keyring.
page.secrets.file: Passwords and keys are kept in a file in the same folder that only your user account can open, because this computer has no password store.
common.pickProject: At the top of the page, choose the project {product}.
common.saveWait: Click Save. Google can take a few minutes to notice.
google.title: Google
google.unset: Sign in with Google to keep your books in Google Drive and to write on phones and tablets at home. Google asks you to set this up once: it is free, takes about ten minutes, and the steps show you where to click. Everyone at home then signs in with their own Google account.
google.working: Everyone you add can sign in with their own Google account.
google.addressesHint: The client in the Google Cloud Console lists each of these under Authorized redirect URIs, exactly as written.
home.title: Phones and tablets at home
home.intro: Phones and tablets on the same Wi-Fi can open {product} too.
home.unset: This computer gets a free name for your home network, and a certificate so phones trust it. It takes about five minutes.
home.waiting: Waiting for you to open the email from deSEC.
home.qrAlt: QR code of the address for phones and tablets
home.shareTitle: Open it on a phone or tablet
home.shareWifi: Connect the phone or tablet to the same Wi-Fi as this computer.
home.shareScan: Point its camera at the code, and tap the link that appears.
home.switchHint: While this is on, this computer answers phones and tablets on your Wi-Fi. It stays on, also after the computer restarts, until you turn it off.
home.stagePublish: deSEC sends the proof that the name is yours to its servers around the world.
home.stageCheck: Let's Encrypt checks the proof and gives the certificate that phones and tablets trust.
terms.first: Phones and tablets trust this computer through a free certificate from Let's Encrypt, a non-profit. {product} asks for it, and renews it, under Let's Encrypt's subscriber agreement. Your acceptance stays valid until Let's Encrypt changes the agreement.
terms.changed: Let's Encrypt asks you to read and accept its agreement again before the next certificate.
terms.keeps: The certificate in use keeps working until it expires.
phones.title: Let phones sign in with Google
phones.hint: Google lets phones sign in only once your client lists this address under Authorized redirect URIs. Open the client, add the address, and save.
port.title: The number at the end of the address
port.intro: Phones reach this computer through a numbered door, called a port. With 443 the address needs nothing at the end; with any other number, the number goes at the end, after a colon.
port.label: Number
port.hint: A new number makes a new address. Phones and tablets then need the new address, Google needs it under Authorized redirect URIs (see Let phones sign in with Google), and work saved only in a phone's browser stays with the old address.
trouble.title: If phones can't connect
trouble.wifi: The phone or tablet must be on the same Wi-Fi as this computer. Guest networks often keep devices apart; use the main one.
trouble.windows: If Windows asks whether to allow {product} on private networks, allow it.
trouble.router: Some routers block names that lead inside the home. In the router's settings, look for DNS rebinding protection and add the name there as an exception.
trouble.address: When the router gives this computer a new address, phones can take up to an hour to find it. To avoid that, ask the router to always give this computer the same address; it may call this address reservation.
trouble.connectionHint: Change it only if this computer is connected in more than one way, for example by cable and by Wi-Fi.
unlink.title: Stop using this name
unlink.body: Phones and tablets can no longer open {product} until you choose a new name. The name and your account stay yours at deSEC.
unlink.forgotten: To look at the account later, sign in on desec.io. Forgot the password? Choose Forgot password there and enter .
know.title: Good to know
know.awake: This computer must stay on and awake while others write.
know.folders: Folders on this computer cannot be opened from a phone. Keep that work in Google Drive.
know.desec: The name comes from deSEC: terms of use, privacy policy.
know.letsencrypt: The certificate comes from Let's Encrypt: subscriber agreement, privacy policy.
know.public: The name is listed publicly, like an entry in a phone book: anyone can look it up, and it appears in the public list of web certificates. All it leads to is this computer's address inside your home, such as 192.168.1.20, which works only on your own Wi-Fi; from anywhere else it leads nowhere. Your books and your writing never pass through deSEC and are never published. deSEC keeps your email address to run the account, and does not publish it. Leave your name, surname and anything else that points to you out of it. That makes the name harder to link to you, but not anonymous: deSEC knows your email address.
others.title: Other settings
login.title: Start at login
login.hint: Starts in the background when you log in to this computer, without opening a window.
login.label: Start {product} at login
browsers.title: Browsers
browsers.hint: Disconnects Google Drive and OpenRouter from every browser, here and on the home network. People stay signed in, with their work on their own device; each connects them again.
browsers.button: Disconnect Google Drive and OpenRouter everywhere
updates.title: Updates
updates.hint: This is version {version}. Checking asks GitHub; nothing is downloaded.
quit.title: Quit
quit.hint: Stops {product} on this computer and on the home network. Saved work stays where it is.
wipe.title: Start over
wipe.hint: Forgets settings so they can be set up again, and disconnects Google Drive and OpenRouter from every browser. Wiping every configuration also removes every password and key kept on this computer. Your project in Google Cloud and your account at deSEC stay.
g1.title: Create a project
g1.openWhy: A project is where Google keeps the sign-in settings for {product}. It is free and asks for no payment details. The first time, Google may ask for your country and to accept its terms.
g1.openDone: Already have a project called {product}? Go on to .
g1.name: For Project name, enter {product}
g1.pickWhy: Google may still show another project, such as My First Project. Made more than one {product} project? Any of them works; a spare project does no harm.
g1.enableWhy: This turns on Google Drive in the project, so {product} can keep your books there.
g1.enableDone: The Google Drive API page ↗ says API enabled, or shows Manage, for the project {product}.
g2.title: Describe the app
g2.startDone: Google shows Overview instead of Get started, and the Branding page ↗ shows the name {product}.
g2.name: For App name, enter {product}
g2.nameWhy: Google shows this name to everyone who signs in.
g2.support: For User support email, choose your own address.
g2.supportWhy: Google shows this address to everyone who signs in.
g2.audienceWhy: External means people with ordinary Google accounts, so it is right for a family. Internal is only for companies with Google Workspace.
g2.contact: For Contact information, enter your own address.
g2.contactWhy: Google writes to this address about the project.
g2.agree: Tick the box to agree, then click Continue and Create.
g3.title: Choose what it may see
g3.openWhy: These permissions let people sign in and keep books in Google Drive. Without them, signing in works but connecting Google Drive is refused.
g3.addDone: The page already lists all five: openid, userinfo.email, userinfo.profile, drive.file and drive.appdata.
g3.paste: Under Manually add scopes, at the bottom of the panel, paste:
g3.pasteWhy: Google lists all five as basic. {product} sees only the files it creates or that you open with it, plus its own hidden settings folder; it cannot see the rest of your Drive.
g3.save: Click Save at the bottom of the page.
g4.title: Choose who can sign in
g4.openWhy: The app stays in Testing: it is listed nowhere and needs no website, and Google lets in only the people on this list. It asks them to reconnect Google Drive every seven days.
g4.people: Enter the Google address of everyone at home who will write, yours too.
g4.peopleWhy: Google lets in no one who isn't on the list, not even you. You can add more people later from the settings.
g4.peopleDone: Every address is listed under Test users.
g5.title: Create the client
g5.existing: Still have the client's file? , or drop it below. If not, make a new client with these steps: Google gives a client's file only once. The new client replaces the old one, so you can delete the old one in Clients afterwards if you like.
g5.openWhy: The client is a pair of keys, an ID and a secret, that tells Google which program is asking.
g5.createDone: Click the client called {product} instead. If there are several, the newest one; a spare client does no harm.
g5.name: For Name, enter {product}
g5.downloadDone: Still have the file? , or drop it below. No file? Copy the Client ID from the right of the client's page, and under Client secrets click Add secret; then .
g5.pasteInstead: Paste the ID and secret instead
g5.lostSecret: Lost the secret? Google shows it only when it is made. Open the client in Clients, click Add secret under Client secrets, and paste the new one here.
g5.done: Google accepts the client. One last step: try signing in.
g6.title: Try signing in
g6.startWhy: One sign-in asks Google about every step at once: the permissions, Google Drive and the client. {product} keeps nothing from it.
g6.unverified: If Google says it hasn't verified the app, click Advanced, then Go to {product}.
g6.unverifiedWhy: Google says this of every app it has not reviewed. Here the app is the Google project that you created yourself.
people.title: Add people who can sign in
people.openWhy: Google lets in only the people listed there.
people.add: Enter the Google address of each new person.
h1.title: Choose a name
h1.emailHint: deSEC sends a link to this address to confirm the account.
h1.name: A name for your home network
h1.nameHint: Phones and tablets find this computer by this name, which deSEC, a non-profit in Berlin, gives for free. Use letters, digits and hyphens. The name is listed publicly, but it leads only to this computer inside your home, and your books never pass through deSEC; leave your name, surname and anything else that points to you out of it.
h1.useExisting: Already have a deSEC account? Use it
hx.title: Use your deSEC name
hx.openWhy: The token lets {product} keep the name pointing at this computer.
hx.plus: Click + to make a new token.
hx.copy: Copy the token deSEC shows; it shows it only once.
hx.name: Your name at deSEC
hx.useNew: Make a new free name instead
h2.title: Save your deSEC password
h2.passwordWhy: It opens your free account at deSEC, which has your email address. You need it only to look at the account on desec.io; {product} forgets it as soon as the name is ready.
h2.saved: I have saved the password in my password manager, or on a note I keep.
h2.limits:
Are the limits of deSEC's free names fine for you?
  • One free name for each person.
  • You cannot move the name to other name servers.
  • The name you chose leads to this computer's address on your home network. deSEC blocks some addresses that were misused in the past: if it blocks this computer's address, the name does not work until the computer has another address.
  • The address behind the name must be updated regularly; {product} updates it each time it turns the home network on.
  • A name not updated for six months is deleted, four weeks after deSEC warns you by email.
  • You read the emails deSEC sends you, and answer when it asks.
h2.accept: With Accept and create the name you accept deSEC's terms of use, which include its privacy policy.
h3.title: Open the email from deSEC
h3.lead: deSEC sends an email to to confirm the account for .
h3.open: Open the email from deSEC. It can take a few minutes; look in the spam folder too.
h3.link: Click the link, which works for 12 hours, and solve deSEC's small picture puzzle. This is the one step {product} cannot do for you.
h3.completed: deSEC then shows a page called Domain Registration Completed, with a token, a password and router settings. You need none of it: don't copy anything, and leave your router as it is. {product} makes its own token and keeps the name up to date by itself. Close deSEC's page and come back here.
h3.slow: No email after a few minutes? If this address already has a deSEC account, deSEC sends nothing new: use that account instead.
h3.done: deSEC confirmed the account: the name is yours. One last step: let phones sign in with Google.
h4.portChoose: To choose the number yourself, use The number at the end of the address on the phones card once you are done here.
h4.openWhy: Google lets phones sign in only at the addresses the client lists, and the phones' address is new.
